summary: Scope: users, conversations and settings (storage.rs, settings.rs, config.rs, main.rs, shutdown.rs, logbuf.rs, logfile.rs, generation.rs, documents.rs, vision.rs, plus the AppState/router/request-context/chat/conversation/settings/memory handlers in api.rs). Overall picture: the backend has no idea who is calling. No record has an owner, and every handler fetches by id with no ownership check. All data goes through ONE SQLite connection behind ONE global lock (93 lock sites), and the code relies on SQLite-only features: rowid ordering, INSERT OR REPLACE, LIMIT -1, PRAGMAs, migrations run on every open, and no foreign keys or cascades. ONE settings object (a JSON blob under the key 'app_settings') is read straight from memory on about 20 request paths. ONE chat reply can run at a time for the whole app: a new message from anyone cancels the running reply, and Stop stops whatever is running. Files (attachments, artifacts, logs) sit in folders next to the program. Startup and shutdown assume this process is the only one: opening the database marks every unfinished task in it as interrupted, and closing writes 'Companion was closed' into every running task. The 18 tables split three ways. Ten hold user data and need an owner, either directly or through their conversation: conversations, messages, message_activities, context_summaries, session_task_context, attachments, artifacts, memory_entries, generation_metrics, model_requests. Three are audit-like and need user and device ids: tool_executions, search_runs, model_requests. Four belong to the model pool manager and are tied to one machine: runtime_calibrations, model_template_caps, runtime_fit_decisions, plus the settings blob's runtime and hardware sections. knowledge_chunks becomes pgvector. Of the settings fields, many are saved but never enforced anywhere: the file size limits, folder limits, network policy, command timeout, log redaction, log level, the output folder and the whole 'advanced' section. Making admin control real is new work, not a move. The chat path (chat_sse) has clear places to add sign-in, the policy checks, document search, the outgoing-data scan, routing and audit (listed in its item). But in code-mode chats, chat itself, and not only the agent, reads the user's project folder: listing, snapshot, read tools, project index, slash commands. The device channel therefore has to serve chat too, not only agent runs.

items.name: AppState (shared server state)
items.what_it_does: Holds everything requests share: the list of models and the one that is loaded, the one model server process, downloads, the one running chat reply, running agent tasks, resource samples, the one settings object, the one permission level, the one database connection, folder locations for models, attachments and artifacts, model load progress, a cache of project indexes and the model fit preparation.
items.change: Split by role. The API server keeps a database pool, a file storage client, a model gateway client, an optional Redis client and a settings resolver. Model list, model server, downloads, load progress and fit preparation move to the model pool manager. The agent registry and project index cache move to the worker. The running chat reply moves to a shared store keyed by generation. Settings and permissions become per-user values worked out on each request, not one shared copy.
items.evidence: pub models: Arc<RwLock<ModelManager>>, llama: Arc<RwLock<LlamaServerManager>>, generations: Arc<RwLock<GenerationTracker>>, settings: Arc<RwLock<AppSettings>>, storage: Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<Storage>>, attachments_dir: PathBuf, repo_index: ...HashMap

items.name: AppState::new_with_dirs / new_with_storage / new_stub
items.what_it_does: Builds the shared state at startup. It reads the saved settings from the database once and works out the permission level from them. It puts the attachments and artifacts folders next to the models folder, and creates one HTTP client for downloads and web search.
items.change: Build from configuration instead: database address, file storage bucket or folder, optional Redis address, sign-in provider. Load no settings at boot; resolve them per request (company default, then group override, then user choice) with a short cache that is cleared when settings change. Remove the folder derivation.

items.name: request_recorder
items.what_it_does: For every model request made by a reply or task, saves the exact request and the model's output in the database in the background, if the privacy switch 'keep a record of model requests' is on.
items.change: Record the user, the conversation owner, the model pool and copy (or outside provider). The switch becomes an admin logging and retention setting that can be locked. Write to PostgreSQL. Retention is handled by a scheduled job on the worker. Only the owner and auditors can read the records. Feed the same event into the audit log.
items.evidence: if !state.settings.read().await.privacy.record_model_requests { return; } state.storage.lock().await.record_model_request(&record)

items.name: AppState::shut_down
items.what_it_does: When the program closes: cancels every running agent task and waits up to 2 seconds. It writes 'stopped because Companion was closed' into each task's reply and marks each task interrupted. Then it cancels the chat reply and stops the model server.
items.change: Replace with a drain for each role. The API server stops taking new requests and tells open reply streams to reconnect. The worker gives back its job leases so another worker continues the task (or it waits as paused); it does not write 'closed' into the user's task. The model pool manager stops its own copies. One server restarting must never touch work owned by other servers.
items.evidence: let unfinished = self.agents.read().await.unfinished(); st.update_message_content(...&message); st.finish_task_context(..., "interrupted"); self.generations.write().await.cancel_current(..); self.llama.write().await.stop().await

items.name: router + trusted_loopback_origins + origin/host guard
items.what_it_does: Lists every web address of the API (about 100 routes, including a /api/v1 copy). It only accepts browser calls from pages served on localhost ports, and rejects any request whose Host header is not a local address. There is no sign-in.
items.change: Add sign-in on every route: a Microsoft Entra ID session or token for people, an API key for software. Add role checks per group of routes. Replace the localhost origin list with configured allowed origins. Move admin routes (model load and unload, downloads, calibration, admin settings, doctor, system metrics) to the admin dashboard API. Move PC-only routes (pick folder, project folders, tool execution, git, diff) behind the desktop app's device channel.
items.evidence: origins = trusted_loopback_origins(); ApiError::new(FORBIDDEN, "Only local Companion hosts are allowed", "...LAN access requires a future authenticated mode."); ["localhost","127.0.0.1","[::1]"]

items.name: chat_sse (the chat request path)
items.what_it_does: Handles one chat message end to end. Slash commands and greetings are answered without the model. It continues a saved task when asked, saves the user's message, and finds the one running model server; with none running it writes an explanation. It decides reasoning and web search from the message, then the conversation, then the global settings, and cancels any other running reply in the app. It summarises old history when the context is nearly full, runs a web search when asked, and for code chats adds project-index hints and local document matches. It streams the model's answer, runs up to 24 rounds of project-reading tools on the backend's disk, and saves plain-text documents as artifacts. At the end it saves the reply, the model used and speed figures.
items.change: Where the new pieces plug in: (1) Sign-in middleware supplies the user before the handler. (2) Ownership check at the conversation lookup (3425-3450). (3) Policy at line 3452, where the global settings are read today: resolve this user's effective settings, check the conversation's model is on the user's allowed list, check the budget before generating. (4) Routing replaces the 'running model server' lookup (3453-3463) and SidecarClient::new(base_url) (3836): the gateway picks the pool for the conversation's model, then the copy by conversation id so the prompt cache is reused, or an outside-provider adapter. (5) Document search replaces knowledge_for/retrieve_knowledge (3767-3806) with a pgvector query over the collections the user may read. (6) Web search (3640-3689) takes provider keys from admin settings and checks the network policy. (7) The outgoing-data scan runs on the final turns just before client.stream (3921), only when the routed target is an outside provider; its decision is audited and can block. (8) Project read tools in code chats (run_chat_tool_round, 3975) go over the device channel to the desktop app, and the reply pauses if the app is offline. (9) Audit records: request accepted, guard decisions, each tool round, completion with token counts (4125-4185). (10) The stream and cancel flag move from an in-process channel and tracker to a shared store (Redis stream when 2+ servers) so another server can resume or stop it. (11) The partial reply is saved at intervals, not only at the end. (12) Remove the global cancel of other replies (3542) and the global 409 while a model loads (3368). (13) Record usage per user for budgets.

items.name: GenerationTracker / ActiveGeneration / cancel_current
items.what_it_does: Tracks exactly one running chat reply: its cancel flag, the text so far, a 'saved already' flag and its background task. Cancelling flags it, kills the task and saves the partial text exactly once.
items.change: Replace with one record per generation in a shared store: owner, conversation, server id, status, last checkpoint. A cancel request reaches whichever server holds the stream. Many generations run at once, with per-user limits. The 'save exactly once' rule becomes a conditional database update.

items.name: Storage struct + open / open_persistent / open_in_memory
items.what_it_does: One SQLite connection to one database file. Opening it creates the folder, sets SQLite options (write-ahead log, 5 s wait for a busy file, memory scratch), runs the schema update and marks unfinished tasks as interrupted, every time.
items.change: Replace with a PostgreSQL connection pool and async methods; about 90 call sites drop the single global lock. Schema updates run once as a deploy step, not on every server start. Interrupted-run recovery moves to the worker. For the single-machine Windows install, ship PostgreSQL (or an embedded one) rather than keeping SQLite as a second code path.

items.name: Storage::migrate (schema and indexes)
items.what_it_does: Creates 18 tables if missing. It adds missing columns by trying to select them and then altering the table, and creates lookup indexes. There are no foreign keys, cascades, full-text search or SQL JSON functions; JSON is stored as text and parsed in code.
items.change: Versioned PostgreSQL migration files. Text dates become timestamptz, 0/1 integers become boolean, JSON text becomes jsonb, REAL becomes double precision. Add owner_id (and device_id where relevant), foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE, and explicit order columns (bigserial) in place of SQLite's hidden row number. Write a one-off importer from existing SQLite files.

items.change: New tables: company settings, group settings (per group), user preferences (per user), and locks (field path, level, who set it). Use jsonb with a version number so servers can drop their cache. Every admin change writes an audit record.

items.change: Owned through the conversation (cascade delete). Add an explicit order column (bigserial or per-conversation sequence) and use it for ordering and truncation. Wrap update plus truncate in one transaction.

items.change: Written by the worker (and API server for chat). Add a bigserial id for order, JSON as jsonb, a foreign key to messages with cascade. Large tool outputs may go to file storage.

items.what_it_does: One running summary per conversation and the ids of the messages it replaces. Used in place of those messages when building model requests.

items.what_it_does: Remembers each code conversation's latest task, its run id, project folder path and status, so 'continue' can resume it.

items.name: Storage::recover_interrupted_activity (startup recovery)
items.what_it_does: Each time the database is opened, marks every 'active' task in the database as interrupted. It also adds an 'Interrupted when the runtime closed' entry to every reply whose journal did not finish, scanning all messages.
items.change: Replace with leases. Each running job has a worker id and a heartbeat; a job counts as interrupted only when its lease expires. Another worker then resumes it, or it waits as 'paused' (also when the desktop app disconnects). Remove from database opening entirely.

items.name: main: listen, graceful shutdown, StopRequest, stop_requested
items.what_it_does: Listens for requests. It reacts to Ctrl+C, window close, Windows sign-out or shutdown, and SIGTERM or SIGHUP by running the close procedure, then exits.
items.change: Keep SIGTERM handling for Kubernetes: stop taking requests, tell open streams to reconnect, give back job leases within the grace period. On a single Windows machine, run as a Windows service and handle service stop, not console-window events.

items.change: Becomes a per-worker 'draining' flag. Tasks are handed to another worker or paused, so the message should say 'paused, will continue', not 'Companion was closed'.

items.what_it_does: List memories visible to a conversation or project; add one (conversation, project or global scope); delete any memory by id; copy a memory into another scope or target id.
items.change: Set and check the owner on every call. 'Global' means this user only. Targets (conversation or project) must belong to the caller. Audit deletions and shares.

surprises.title: Only one chat reply can run in the whole app; any new message cancels it
surprises.why_it_matters: With many users, user B sending a message stops user A's reply mid-stream, and any user's Stop stops whoever is generating. Stop and session actions take no owner. Chat is also refused with 409 for everyone while any model loads. The single-slot tracker has to be replaced (one record per generation, shared cancel flag), not just moved behind a lock.
surprises.evidence: chat_sse: s.generations.write().await.cancel_current(&s.storage).await ("A new turn supersedes any running one"); GenerationTracker { current: Option<ActiveGeneration> }; chat_stop has no conversation parameter; s.runtime_update.try_lock() → CONFLICT

surprises.title: Opening the database marks every unfinished task as interrupted
surprises.why_it_matters: With several API servers and workers sharing one PostgreSQL, a restart of any one process would mark every other process's live tasks as interrupted and cancelled. Recovery has to become lease or heartbeat based on the worker, and must come out of the database-open path.
surprises.evidence: open_persistent → s.recover_interrupted_activity(); UPDATE session_task_context SET status='interrupted' WHERE status='active'; appends AgentState::Cancelled 'Interrupted when the runtime closed' to every unfinished journal

surprises.title: No ownership checks anywhere; every record is reachable by id
surprises.why_it_matters: Once more than one user exists, any signed-in user could read, delete or post into anyone's conversations, artifacts, attachments and memories by id. share_conversation writes into any target conversation, post_message accepts assistant and tool roles (forged replies), and the 'global' memory scope reaches every user's prompts. Adding owner_id to the tables is not enough: every one of the ~60 handlers in scope needs an owner filter, which suggests one shared 'load conversation for this user' helper.
surprises.evidence: get_artifact: SELECT ... FROM artifacts WHERE id=?; delete_memory: DELETE FROM memory_entries WHERE id=?; memories_for: WHERE scope='global' OR ...; validate_role accepts "assistant" | "tool"

surprises.title: Conversation export carries the whole program's log
surprises.why_it_matters: A user's export includes the last 1,000 log lines of the process, which with many users means other users' activity (ids, errors, model loads). With several servers it is also only one server's partial log. Remove it from user exports.

surprises.title: The web search key is sent to the browser
surprises.why_it_matters: GET /api/settings returns the whole settings object, including search.brave_key; only the /config chat command hides it. The design gives search keys to the admin, so secrets need their own store and must never be returned by any user-facing settings endpoint.
surprises.evidence: async fn get_settings(...) { Json(s.settings.read().await.clone()) } vs config_text: v["search"]["brave_key"] = "***"

surprises.title: Many admin-owned settings in the design are stored but never enforced today
surprises.why_it_matters: Folder limits (allowed_dirs, blocked_dirs), network policy and trusted hosts, the command timeout, file size limits, OCR switch, log redaction, telemetry, log level, output_dir and the whole 'advanced' section are never read by the backend (or the frontend). The real limits are constants: 5 MB attachments, 8 MB pictures, 20 MB artifacts. The plan must count enforcing these (in the desktop app, gateway and upload paths) as new work, not a move.
surprises.evidence: grep max_attach_mb|allowed_dirs|blocked_dirs|trusted_hosts|log_redaction|command_timeout_secs|output_dir|server_port|parallel_sessions → only settings.rs; add_attachment const MAX_ATTACH_BYTES: usize = 5_000_000

surprises.title: Chat itself, not only the agent, touches the user's project folder
surprises.why_it_matters: The design sends agent tools over the device channel. But code-mode chat also reads the PC directly: the project listing and instructions file go into every prompt, up to 24 rounds of read and search tools run in chat, the project index and document chunks come from the folder, and /search, /find and /diff run on the backend's disk. The device channel must serve the API server's chat path too, with request-response timing inside a live reply, or chat must hand code questions to a worker.
surprises.evidence: assemble_request_context → workspace_snapshot(std::fs::read_dir); chat_sse → run_chat_tool_round(...), cached_repo_index(..), st.knowledge_for(ws_id); run_slash_command "diff" → crate::terminal::run(SAFE_GIT_DIFF_STAT, &ws, 30); command_workspace accepts any typed path that is_dir()

surprises.title: Changing the permission mode changes it for everyone and approves other people's waiting actions
surprises.why_it_matters: put_permission_mode and put_settings set one approval level for the whole process, then release every waiting approval the new mode allows across all tasks. In a multi-user system, one user switching to Auto would approve other users' pending file edits. Mode, cap and release have to be per user, with release signalled to the worker that holds the run.
surprises.evidence: s.permissions.write().await.autonomy = autonomy; resume_auto_approved_runs iterates registry.summaries() for every WaitingPermission run

surprises.title: All database access is serialised through one connection and one lock, and the access layer is synchronous
surprises.why_it_matters: 93 places take the single tokio Mutex on one rusqlite connection; each request holds it while doing several queries, sometimes across awaits on other locks. Moving to PostgreSQL is not a driver swap: the access layer becomes async with a pool, every call site changes, and multi-step updates need explicit transactions (fork, edit-and-truncate, delete cascade, compaction check-then-save). Size this as L on its own.
surprises.evidence: pub storage: Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<Storage>>; pub struct Storage { conn: Connection }; Grep count storage.lock(): api.rs 83, agent_runner.rs 7, generation.rs 3

surprises.title: SQLite-only behaviour the PostgreSQL move must replace
surprises.why_it_matters: Order and truncation depend on SQLite's hidden row number (messages, activities, attachments, artifacts, metrics). There are SQLite PRAGMAs, INSERT OR REPLACE, 'LIMIT -1 OFFSET', 0/1 integers as booleans, text timestamps, JSON in text columns, and a home-made 'add column if missing' migration run on every open. There are no foreign keys, so deleting a conversation orphans artifacts, metrics, summaries, journals, model request records, search records, memories and every file on disk. No full-text search or SQL JSON functions are used, which makes the move simpler.
surprises.evidence: ORDER BY rowid; rowid > (SELECT rowid ...); a.rowid=(SELECT MAX(rowid) ...); INSERT OR REPLACE INTO ...; LIMIT -1 OFFSET ?; PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; SELECT {column} FROM {table} LIMIT 0

surprises.title: Model request records are trimmed globally, and 'owner_id' there means a reply id, not a person
surprises.why_it_matters: Every insert trims the whole table to 300 rows and about 50 MB. With many users only minutes of history survive, and one heavy user removes everyone else's records. These rows hold full prompts (sensitive) and are on by default. The existing column name owner_id clashes with the new 'every record has an owner' rule; rename it before adding user ownership.
surprises.evidence: pub const MODEL_REQUEST_ROWS: usize = 300; pub const MODEL_REQUEST_BYTES: usize = 50_000_000; /// The reply message or agent run the request belonged to. pub owner_id: String

surprises.title: Chat and context screens are built around 'the current loaded model'
surprises.why_it_matters: Replies go to whichever model is running, not the conversation's chosen model. Vision support, the context window, the speed figures' model id and the 'stale model' recovery list all read the one current model. With several models served, the conversation's model_id must drive routing and the ability profile, and the 'stale / resume / discard' recovery flow loses its meaning.
surprises.evidence: s.models.read().await.current().map(|m| m.vision); llama.running.as_ref().map(|r| (r.base_url.clone(), r.cfg.clone())); sessions_recovery filter c.last_model != loaded; chat_sse saves st.set_last_model(&cid, &model) from models.current()

surprises.title: A reply in progress lives only in the API server's memory until it ends
surprises.why_it_matters: The streamed text is kept in memory and saved only on completion or Stop. A server crash or a rolling deploy loses the whole partial reply, and a client that reconnects to another server cannot pick the stream up. The stateless-server design needs periodic checkpoints and a shared stream (Redis when 2+ servers), plus a rule for who finishes a reply when its server dies.
surprises.evidence: let partial = Arc::new(Mutex::new(String::new())); ... st.add_message(... content: stored ...) only after the loop; Sse::new(UnboundedReceiverStream::new(rx))

surprises.title: Same-name attachments overwrite each other on disk
surprises.why_it_matters: Attachment bytes are stored under conversation folder + file name, so uploading 'notes.txt' twice keeps two records but one file. Moving to file storage should key by attachment id; existing data needs care during import.
surprises.evidence: let dir = s.attachments_dir.join(&id); std::fs::write(dir.join(&safe), &bytes); attachment_file reads attachments_dir.join(&id).join(&att.filename)

surprises.title: Settings read on request paths outside this job's files
surprises.why_it_matters: Other jobs must also switch these reads to 'this user's effective settings' or 'this pool's settings': prepare_fits (api.rs 1673), start_sidecar (1869), execute_tool (5417), run_agent (5859), runtime_policy (8870), calibrate_model (9814), and agent_runner.rs 2832, 3859 and 4838 (compaction policy and settings clones inside the agent loop, which will run on the worker).

surprises.title: The default thread count is measured on whichever machine creates the settings
surprises.why_it_matters: AppSettings::default detects the processor of the machine running the backend. In the target, that is the API server, not the machine running the model copies, so default tuning would be wrong. Hardware defaults belong to the pool manager on each node.
